new_statements.quote: (thesis p.5, 'Explanation of orthography', pdf p.6:) "Some problems remain unsolved in the phonology, and further study is needed before a thorough phonological statement can be made. The orthography may be described in terms of the syllable. Each syllable must have a vowel and a tone." (thesis pp.20-21, section 3.12 'Exponents of elements of sentence structure', pdf pp.41-42:) "The final element is the place of operation of a class of final particles. These are usually accompanied by very weak stress, together with a certain amount of centralisation of the vowels, making it very hard to determine their actual phonological form. It may be better to consider that different systems of vowels and tones operate in these particles from those which operate in the rest of the language." new_statements.relation_note: new: nothing on record (no catalog record, no stress statement held by the project for tayy1238). What it adds is marginal: tone on every syllable plus unstressed (weakly stressed) sentence-final particles; it gives no word-stress placement, so it neither supports nor contradicts any fixed-position reading. Compatible with the 'silent on stress' readings of the seven sources already read.
new_statements.rule_in_words: A syntax thesis with only an orthography-and-phonology sketch: Tho (Tay) is described as tonal, every syllable carrying one of six tones (high rising; high rising glottalised; mid level; low rising; mid falling / mid falling glottalised; low level or low falling; one tone only in a few Vietnamese loans). The only remark on stress is that sentence-final particles are 'usually accompanied by very weak stress' with centralised vowels, possibly with a reduced vowel/tone system of their own. No rule for the placement of stress within polysyllabic words (e.g. phep-tac, p'o-me, p.36) is given, and the author says a thorough phonological statement remains to be made.
new_statements.exceptions: sentence-final particles: very weak stress, centralised vowels, tones hard to determine; the sixth (low level/low falling, no final stop) tone occurs only in a few Vietnamese loans; focus particle ni- followed by a slight pause and 'seems to throw emphasis of some kind on the preceding unit' (p.20).
new_statements.identity_note: Day's data come from a single speaker, Hoàng Chung Minh (aged 56), who had lived most of his life at Kỳ Lừa just outside Lạng Sơn town (north-eastern Vietnam) and was recorded in the refugee resettlement village of Tùng Nghĩa, Tuyên Đức province (South Vietnam), early 1960s; the speaker called his language Thô or Tày as opposed to Nùng / Phàn Slình (thesis p.30). This is the Lạng Sơn Tày variety, the same area as Gordaliza 1908.

new_statements.quote: [p. I] Les Tày du Tonkin, comme ceux de Chine et du Laos, parlent une langue monosyllabique et tonique. [p. II] La langue tày comprend cinq tons ou intonations ... [p. III] Malgré la ressemblance des tons, il y a une grande différence entre la prononciation annamite et la prononciation tày. D'abord, le ton de la voix est d'ordinaire beaucoup plus élevé chez le tày que chez l'annamite, ce qui donne à la conversation un ton particulier ; ensuite, le tày accentue moins que l'annamite, et parle plus vite. Il lui arrive souvent d'escamoter la dernière voyelle d'une syllable, la voyelle a particulièrement
new_statements.translation: [p. I] The Tày of Tonkin, like those of China and Laos, speak a monosyllabic and tonal language. [p. II] The Tày language has five tones or intonations ... [p. III] Despite the resemblance of the tones, there is a great difference between Annamite (Vietnamese) and Tày pronunciation. First, the pitch of the voice is ordinarily much higher with the Tày than with the Annamite, which gives conversation a particular tone; next, the Tày accentuates less than the Annamite and speaks faster. He often drops the last vowel of a syllable, the vowel a in particular.

new_statements.relation_note: new: nothing on record. First statement for tayy1238: tonal (five tones) per an older primary description; only an impressionistic 'accentue moins que l'annamite', no word-stress placement rule. The bib_tag 'likely states stress' is not borne out: the Précis has a tone section but no stress section.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tày (Clear-River 'Tày blancs') is described as a monosyllabic tone language with five tones (phiêng level, tấm rising, lùng falling, khảm 'interrogative', nặm low), lacking the Vietnamese ngã tone. The only remark touching accent is impressionistic and comparative: Tày 'accentuates less' than Vietnamese, is spoken at a higher pitch and faster, and often drops a syllable's final vowel. No statement of where word stress falls, and nothing on stress in disyllables or compounds.
new_statements.exceptions: none about stress. Notes: Vietnamese ngã tone 'n'existe pas en tày' (p. III); p. V on the diphthong ay 'l'a est très bref, tout le son se porte sur l'y' is syllable-internal vowel prominence, not word stress; final-vowel elision (thua > thu, khua > khu, mia > mi) p. III.
new_statements.identity_note: Savina describes the speech of the 'Tày blancs' of the upper region of Tonkin, 'particulièrement, le bassin de la rivière claire' (Préface p. I), i.e. Clear-River basin Tày = Central Tai Tày (tayy1238); the copy consulted sits in the taid1250 (Tai Dón / White Tai of Lai Châu) folder only because the compilers filed it there, and that reader's own notes (Gedney 1964 p. 416, Donaldson 1963 p. 2) already say Savina's 'Tay' is an eastern/Central-Tai variety, not Lai Châu Tai Dón. Transcription is quốc-ngữ based; Savina says dialects vary by tribe and place.

sources.note: Chương II 'Ngữ âm' (pp. 15-25) treats articulators, syllable template (âm đầu/âm đệm/âm gốc/âm cuối + thanh điệu), 11+3 vowels, consonants, six tones (§6 p. 24: bằng, sắc, huyền, hỏi, nặng, lửng) and tone-rhyme co-occurrence; the term 'trọng âm' (stress) never occurs; the reduplication section (pp. 39-41) mentions only 'ngữ điệu bình thường' (normal intonation) vs emphatic lengthening. Silent on word stress.
